items.def: Algorithms train models using labeled data (each input set has a corresponding output label); divided into classification (assign inputs to predefined classes) and ML regression (predict continuous numerical values). Note: ML regression differs from 'regression' in other ISTQB syllabi (change-related defects).

Trains models on unlabeled data, inferring patterns or structures; categorized into clustering (grouping by similarities, e.g., customer segments) and association (identifying relationships/dependencies among attributes, e.g., purchasing patterns for recommendations).

An intelligent agent learns by interacting with its environment, receiving rewards or penalties based on action outcomes — learning from experience rather than a dataset. Challenges: setting up the environment, designing the reward function, selecting the best strategy.
Carried out alongside data preparation to discover trends, patterns, and anomalies and to visualize data using plots and charts.
Training: used to train the model. Validation: used for evaluating and subsequently tuning the model. Test (holdout): used to test the tuned model — independent of training and validation.

For limited data: divide the combined training+validation pool into k folds (commonly 5 or 10, typically random, often stratified); train on k-1 folds, validate on the held-out fold, repeat k times; average the fold metrics, then train the final model on the whole pool and evaluate once on the hold-out test set.

Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained neural network to a new task with much less training data/effort than building from scratch; tuning may apply to the entire network, specific layers (typically near the output end), or additional layers. Success depends on similarity between original and new tasks.

Provides task-specific data sources to the LLM: transformed into a searchable format, relevant documents are incorporated into an enhanced prompt — more precise responses with NO change to the pretrained model.

Activation value: the output of an activation function of a neuron (computed from a weighted sum of previous-layer activations plus the neuron's bias). Epoch: an iteration of ML training on the whole training dataset.
Model hyperparameters define the model structure (e.g., number of neural-network layers, decision-tree depth); algorithm hyperparameters control the training (e.g., number of training iterations).

items.text: ML workflow activities (Figure 1 order): Understand the Objectives (agree purpose + acceptance criteria incl. ML functional performance metrics) → Select a Framework → Select & Build the Algorithm → Prepare & Test Data (acquisition, preprocessing, feature engineering + EDA; data must be representative of operational data) → Train → Evaluate (on validation dataset; several models/algorithms typically compared) → Tune (adjust model + algorithm hyperparameters, retrain) — Train/Evaluate/Tune = 'model generation' cycle → Test the Model (independent test dataset; significantly lower performance than evaluation → return to model generation or data prep) → Deploy (re-engineered with data pipeline; re-tested) → Use (batch or real-time) → Monitor & Tune. Failures often originate in earlier steps such as data preparation or model selection.

Pretrained/RAG: fine-tuning needs task similarity (cat→dog breeds works; images→accents doesn't); a pretrained model can use RAG, fine-tuning, or both; biases or vulnerabilities in the pretrained model carry over to the new model — testing needed for the new task.

Data preparation = data acquisition (identify types, gather from databases/APIs/sensors, label for supervised) + preprocessing (clean: remove defects/duplicates/outliers, impute missing values mean/median/mode, anonymize; transform/scale/normalize; augment incl. adversarial examples and synthetic data; sample subsets) + feature engineering (select relevant, extract informative non-redundant features), with EDA in parallel. Iterative, often manual, reorderable. Operational data should match training-data characteristics (distributions, feature ranges).

Dataset splits: amounts depend on model complexity, algorithm, resources (RAM/disk/compute/time), desired confidence. Limited data → hold-out test set + k-fold cross-validation on the rest (average metrics = generalization estimate; final model trained on full pool, evaluated once on hold-out); leave-one-out (k = number of samples) and bootstrap are other resampling options; without any hold-out, cross-validation averages are optimistically biased.

Deep neural network: input layer (receives inputs) → hidden layers (neurons/nodes) → output layer (results to outside world); fully connected = each neuron connects to all neurons in the next layer. Each neuron computes a weighted sum of previous-layer activations plus its own bias, passed through a non-linear activation function (this bias is unrelated to 5.1.2's fairness bias). Weights/biases initialized to small random values (biases sometimes zero); error/loss fed back to adjust them; each pass through the training dataset = an epoch; training ends when output is good enough.

Neural network coverage: Neuron Coverage (proportion of neurons whose output exceeds a threshold during testing); k-Multisection Neuron Coverage kMNC (each neuron's output range divided into k sections; proportion of sections activated); Neuron Boundary Coverage NBC (proportion of neurons whose output exceeds the training maximum or falls below the training minimum). Value: reveals untested areas; limits: structural coverage alone doesn't guarantee generalization (spurious correlations → correct activations for wrong reasons) — combine with adversarial and metamorphic testing.

items.name: Precision
items.note: Proportion of positives that were correctly predicted — how sure one can be about positive predictions.

items.name: Recall (sensitivity)
items.note: Proportion of actual positives correctly predicted — confidence that no positives will be missed.

items.name: F1-score
items.note: Harmonic mean of precision and recall, 0–100; close to 100 = both high (FP and FN minimal impact).

items.text: Precision divides by predicted positives (TP+FP) — 'how sure about positive predictions'; recall divides by actual positives (TP+FN) — 'no positives missed'. Both use TP as numerator; swapping denominators is the classic exam error.

Validation drives evaluation AND tuning (may be reused in iterations); test is the independent holdout used once on the tuned model to confirm criteria. Significantly lower test performance than evaluation signals overfitting-style trouble → return to model generation.

Fine-tuning changes the pretrained model via additional task-specific training (needs similarity between tasks); RAG leaves the model unchanged and injects relevant retrieved documents into an enhanced prompt.

Supervised learns from labeled datasets (input→label mapping); reinforcement learns from environment interaction via rewards/penalties — 'from experience rather than from a dataset'. Unsupervised finds structure in unlabeled data (clustering/association).

items.confusion: Neuron Coverage vs kMNC vs NBC
items.text: NC: neuron outputs above a threshold; kMNC: k sections per neuron's output range, proportion activated; NBC: outputs beyond the training-time maximum/minimum. NBC detects inputs outside training experience; kMNC grades activation granularity.
Model = structure (layers, tree depth); algorithm = training controls (iteration count). Tuning (3.1.2) adjusts both.
